text: Eu-Tong-Sen: The Eu Yan Sang King Whose Name Is on the Street
He worked collecting debts for a grocery shop, drifted into the tin country of Perak, and in 1879, in the mining town of Gopeng, he opened a small shop selling traditional Chinese medicine.

In 1882 Eu Kong obtained a general tax farm for the Batang Padang district — a licence to collect the government's taxes on opium, gambling, alcohol and pawnbroking — and it was the farm's revenues that financed his tin mines and the growth of the medicine business.
By 1908 he owned 11 mines — eight in Perak, two in Selangor, one in Negri Sembilan — employing some 12,000 workers, and he was known as the King of Tin.
Singapore followed in 1910, at 265 to 271 South Bridge Road: a row of four shophouses designed by Alfred Bidwell of Swan and Maclaren, the architect of the Raffles Hotel.

In 1918 he improved part of the street, adding a bridge, railings for the monsoon drains and back lanes for theatres, and in 1919 the street was renamed Eu-Tong-Sen Street — in his lifetime, when he was about 42.

In 1927 his own theatre rose on the street at number 80: the Majestic, built as Tien Yien Moh Toi, a Cantonese opera house with an Art Deco façade of glazed tiles, blue dragons and opera figures, designed by Swan and Maclaren.
The college named three of its buildings for its great donors, and one of them, a student hostel around the Upper Quadrangle, took his name: the Eu-Tong-Sen Building.
On the 11th of May 1941, at Sirmio, Eu-Tong-Sen died of heart failure, aged 63.

In 1993 Richard Eu led the family's buyback of the medicine business for 21 million Singapore dollars, re-incorporated it in Singapore as Eu Yan Sang International, folded the Hong Kong arm back in during 1996 and 1997 — reuniting the two halves for the first time in more than 50 years — and listed the group on the SGX mainboard in July 2000.
In June 2024 it changed hands again: Japan's Rohto Pharmaceutical took about 60 per cent and Mitsui about 30 per cent, in a deal valuing the company at roughly 808 million Singapore dollars.

But the smallest thing his family built — one medicine shop in a Perak tin town, opened by his father in 1879 — is still open for business, 147 years on: Japanese-owned, Singapore-headquartered, and chaired by his grandson.
